speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- FREEDOM OF CHIEF JUSTICE OF QUEBEC TO INTERVIEW MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Justice? Without accepting the position of the government that the chief justice of the province of Quebec should be asked to act as conscience of the government in place of the Prime Minister, may I ask if the chief justice will be completely free to interview ministers and obtain ministerial papers, documents or other permanent records?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- FREEDOM OF CHIEF JUSTICE OF QUEBEC TO INTERVIEW MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, without accepting the premise of the hon. member's question, may I say this: the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec has been asked, as I think is proper and in line with my view of the independence of the judiciary and separation of powers, to indicate to me any information that he feels it is appropriate to give me relating to unwarranted attempts to interfere with the proper administration of justice in his courts.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- FREEDOM OF CHIEF JUSTICE OF QUEBEC TO INTERVIEW MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister did not answer my question. I was asking about the position of the government. For example, the Minister of Public Works raised the matter of privilege with respect to conversations he had with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I ask the minister if the chief justice will be given the opportunity to interview the Minister of Public Works and other ministers with respect to any intervention, alleged or otherwise, with the judiciary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- FREEDOM OF CHIEF JUSTICE OF QUEBEC TO INTERVIEW MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that if the chief justice of the Superior Court wants to do that, the ministers and members of the government will co-operate fully.

I had a conversation, also with the associate chief justice of Quebec, along, as I discovered, with a great many other public spirited citizens
who had taken part in trying to effect a solution to a rather difficult and, to some degree, unprecedented problem.

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REFERENCE TO INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be particularly helpful if one were to try to anticipate what may be the views formulated by the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec.

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- RECOMMENDATIONS OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE CONCERNING INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- RECOMMENDATIONS OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE CONCERNING INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Justice, the chief legal officer of Canada, with regard to the confession of the Minister of Public Works. That minister, when answering me on Wednesday last said, in part, as reported on page 11457 of Hansard:
Indeed, the only intervention that would be contemplated by me would be one to see that he was in full knowledge of the facts-
Meaning the judge, the minister having been in touch with the associate chief justice. I continue-
-and did his duty.
My question to the chief law officer of Canada, Attorney General and Minister of Justice, is this: has the minister, in view of the confession made by the Minister of Public Works that he intervened, and tried to tell the judge how to do his duty, made recommendations to the Prime Minister? Has he made any recommendations relating to the impropriety of the executive engaging in that kind of intervention with the judiciary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- RECOMMENDATIONS OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE CONCERNING INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Public Works went on to say, again as reported at page 11457 of Hansard:
I did not attempt to influence the decision.
As I indicated on Wednesday, although Mr. Justice Mackay's letter asked me to take no action I felt it incumbent on me to ask my colleagues for an explanation, which I received. The information indicates no attempt on their part to interfere with the course of justice.

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- RECOMMENDATIONS OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE CONCERNING INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING LEGAL OPINION ON INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING LEGAL OPINION ON INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext:
Yesterday the Minister of Justice answered a question put by the hon. member for St. John's East. He pointed out two matters that would be crimes under the Code, one of which would be and I quote from page 11489 of Hansard:
-to have a private communication for the purpose of influencing a judicial decision.
It is easy for a fellow to say he did not influence the jury. It is similar to defending someone for murder. I have never heard anyone tell his counsel he was guilty. The facts determine whether he is guilty. In light of the two points of law raised in the minister's answer to the hon. member for St. John's East, has he referred those two matters to his legal officers in view of the self confession of interference by the Minister of Public Works?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING LEGAL OPINION ON INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the words I was using yesterday are from Halsbury's definition of the nature of private communications, which amounts to criminal contempt. As the hon. member knows, that is a proceeding to be taken by a judge. In all three instances, no such proceedings have been taken.

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING LEGAL OPINION ON INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know that the Minister of Justice will want to answer this question. Is he prepared to refer the matter to his legal officers? I respect Halsbury's Laws of England. However, as the chief legal officer of Canada, is the minister prepared to refer the matter to his legal officers to get an opinion rather than just refer to certain precedents and come to his own decisions without an opinion from his legal officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- POSSIBILITY OF OBTAINING LEGAL OPINION ON INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: As an eminent lawyer in Calgary, I think the hon. member knows that contempt proceedings are not taken at the instance of the Attorney General of Canada, but at the instance of the judge himself. No such proceedings have been taken. In answer to the hon. member, I may indicate that in the course of my duties, I have many communications with chief justices throughout Canada on a whole range of matters relating to salaries, retirement, workloads and work with the judicial council. In no instance has any chief justice ever brought to my attention an attempt to interfere with the course of justice by members of the ministry.

subtopic: SUMMER GAMES AT ST. JOHN'S-FAILURE TO CALL TENDERS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF MAIN SPORTS COMPLEX-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I will direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister. It concerns the summer games that are to be held

in St. John's, Newfoundland, in 1977. As the Acting Prime Minister is aware, the federal government will be spending several million dollars as their share in the financing of these games. Is the Acting Prime Minister aware that the contract involving the principal expenditure of some $4.5 million for a main sports complex has been granted to a company without going through public tender?

subtopic: SUMMER GAMES AT ST. JOHN'S-FAILURE TO CALL TENDERS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF MAIN SPORTS COMPLEX-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SUMMER GAMES AT ST. JOHN'S-FAILURE TO CALL TENDERS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF MAIN SPORTS COMPLEX-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was not aware of that fact.

subtopic: SUMMER GAMES AT ST. JOHN'S-FAILURE TO CALL TENDERS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF MAIN SPORTS COMPLEX-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Both local councillors and a local newspaper have raised this issue with particular reference to the fact that the company which got the contract without tender is in fact owned by Mr. Andrew Crosbie who is chairman of the summer games association. Is it the Prime Minister's view that this procedure is appropriate, bearing in mind the fact that in the past public tendering for the summer games has been a condition insisted on by the federal government, as I understand it?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SUMMER GAMES AT ST. JOHN'S-FAILURE TO CALL TENDERS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF MAIN SPORTS COMPLEX-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I will inquire into the circumstances. I understand it is not suggested that the federal government is awarding this contract. Do I understand correctly that it is some other authority which was awarded the contract?

subtopic: SUMMER GAMES AT ST. JOHN'S-FAILURE TO CALL TENDERS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF MAIN SPORTS COMPLEX-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: The minister is correct in that assumption, according to my information; the contract has been awarded by the local committee. Nevertheless, a substantial portion of the money is coming from the federal government, approximately one-third, hence the reason for concern on the part of the federal government. Would the Acting Prime Minister undertake to make an inquiry and ascertain why calling for tenders was not insisted upon by the federal government, though this was the case in the past, and, more specifically, will he investigate the possibility of a conflict of interest in view of the fact that a contract was awarded to a company owned by the chairman of the summer games committee?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SUMMER GAMES AT ST. JOHN'S-FAILURE TO CALL TENDERS FOR CONSTRUCTION OF MAIN SPORTS COMPLEX-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I will undertake to make those inquiries, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- INQUIRY WHETHER LEGAL OPINION SOUGHT ON INTERVENTION BY PRIME MINISTER'S PRINCIPAL SECRETARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice dealing with the Prime Minister's conclusion that a lawyer, who was also principal secretary to the Prime Minister, made a legitimate intervention.
The minister realizes that there is a cardinal rule that there should be no intervention by anyone, particularly by lawyers, during the course of a trial by a judge. Was the then minister of justice asked for an opinion as to this course of action by a lawyer and in particular was the hon. gentleman's opinion sought before the Prime Minister con-
March 5, 1976

eluded that this was a legitimate intervention, and, if so, what was the advice given?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- INQUIRY WHETHER LEGAL OPINION SOUGHT ON INTERVENTION BY PRIME MINISTER'S PRINCIPAL SECRETARY
speechtext: With respect to the first part of the question, because all this was seven years ago, we are endeavouring to determine the answer to that question. With regard to the second part of the question, the explanation by the then principal secretary, now Minister of National Health and Welfare, was provided to myself and to the Prime Minister. As the Prime Minister explained yesterday, it was a request on behalf of a foreign government which was concerned about matters in its own country and wished to know the date when a judgment would be made, and that was the purpose for the communication with the judge.

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REQUEST THAT OPINION OF BAR BE OBTAINED ON RULES FOR INTERVENTION BY LAWYERS
ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REQUEST THAT OPINION OF BAR BE OBTAINED ON RULES FOR INTERVENTION BY LAWYERS
speechtext:
In the
light of the dangerous precedent set by the Prime Minister in terms of his calling the intervention a legitimate one, would the hon. gentleman contact all bar associations and law societies throughout the country to get an opinion on interventions of this sort and to determine whether there is one rule for lawyers who are members of parliament or who work in the Prime Minister's office or for the government and another for lawyers not so engaged?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REQUEST THAT OPINION OF BAR BE OBTAINED ON RULES FOR INTERVENTION BY LAWYERS
speechtext: I think the Prime Minister made the position very clear yesterday, both inside and outside this chamber, that all ministers and members of the House are expected to obey the law just as any other citizen.

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REQUEST THAT OPINION OF BAR BE OBTAINED ON RULES FOR INTERVENTION BY LAWYERS
speechtext: Would the minister kindly answer my question? This is an extremely important matter. Bar associations throughout the country will be extremely concerned. I ask him again whether he will take this matter up with the presidents of the bar associations and law societies so as to make sure there are not two rules affecting lawyers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ALLEGATIONS OF INTERFERENCE BY JUDGE MACKAY- REQUEST THAT OPINION OF BAR BE OBTAINED ON RULES FOR INTERVENTION BY LAWYERS
speechtext: I would be happy to receive any views the bar or the law societies might wish to send me, but with all due respect to the hon. member's question I do not need the advice of the bar to know that members of this House and members of the government are expected, like other citizens, to obey the law.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO IMPROVE GROWTH OF GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Since it appears that the worst GNP growth performance since 1954 indicates a complete lack of confidence in the economic management of the federal government, may I ask the minister whether he can explain what steps the govern-
Oral Questions
ment is taking to improve the growth performance in the economic sector, or is the government committing the country to zero growth for the forseeable future, or certainly for the next few months?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO IMPROVE GROWTH OF GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would invite the hon. gentleman to read with some care the Statistics Canada analysis of March 4 of the figures for 1975. He will note, as I have stated many times in the House during the past several months, that the principal underperformance of the economy has been in the export sector, particularly because of the slow recovery of the major export markets such as the United States, Japan and western Europe from the much deeper recession that they went into than did Canada.
We notice that in terms of domestic products, for example in the durables sector, and indeed with the recent spectacular increase in the housing sector, the economy in Canada itself is very clearly responding to the measures that my predecessor put forward and that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs in charge of housing put forward to assist the domestic economy. However, we have to be concerned at the recovery of world markets upon whose success the economic success of Canada is so dependent.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO IMPROVE GROWTH OF GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The most significant news in that the pace of growth in the last quarter was only one-third the pace of the growth in the previous three months, so certainly I would question the minister's statement of a few moments ago. Since it seems to indicate that Canada is having a very difficult time coming out of its own recession, is the government contemplating the updating of its spring budget in order to deal with the serious matter of Canada's very sluggish economy?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO IMPROVE GROWTH OF GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the best I can do is to read to the hon. gentleman what Statistics Canada had to say about the fourth quarter:
The fourth quarter weakness was reflected by a very moderate 1.6 per cent increase in wages, salaries and supplementary labour income, which is by far the largest component of gross national product.
Then, reading on:
However, to some extent this weakness is misleading, since it follows the payment of large cost of living allowances in the third quarter; these payments had the effect of raising the third quarter growth rate at the expense of the fourth, and, if they were excluded, the fourth quarter growth would have been a much more normal 3.5 per cent.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO IMPROVE GROWTH OF GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT
speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The minister has not answered my question. The real gross national product rose by only 0.2 per cent in 1975, which Statistics Canada has indicated is the worst GNP growth performance since 1954. Is the government intending to continue on the same course it has followed over the past few months, or is it contemplating bringing in an earlier than anticipated budget to deal with the very sluggish performance of the Canadian economy at the present time?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO IMPROVE GROWTH OF GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can only state to the hon. gentleman that he might study more carefully the Statistics Canada report. I think he would have a better understanding of the current state of the economy, and indeed of the circumstances under which

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN CROWN LIABILITY PROVISION WHEN INJURY CAUSED BY RADIOACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. Is consideration being given by the government to amending the limitation period under which the Crown and Crown agencies can be sued to make it crystal clear that in cases of physical or medical injury to persons arising from radioactivity the limitation period only starts running when knowledge of the damage becomes known and not when knowledge of the radioactivity or cause of the injury occurs? Am I making myself clear? In other words, will it be made certain that a lawsuit need not be started until it is obvious that injury has occurred as distinct from having to sue when knowledge of the exposure occurs?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN CROWN LIABILITY PROVISION WHEN INJURY CAUSED BY RADIOACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question or the issue is clear to me. I indicated at a meeting of Attorneys General in Halifax last October that I was considering revisions to both the Federal Court Act and the Crown Liability Act. That consideration is still underway. I am not in a position to say at this point when I will be able to make recommendations to my colleagues or when legislation might be introduced. However, the issue the hon. member's question raised is under consideration.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN CROWN LIABILITY PROVISION WHEN INJURY CAUSED BY RADIOACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if it would be possible for the minister to put this on a rather higher priority than it obviously is at the moment, because the issue is very topical in certain areas of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGE IN CROWN LIABILITY PROVISION WHEN INJURY CAUSED BY RADIOACTIVITY

REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED
subsubtopic: FISH IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Fisheries. In view of the profound effect of the restrictions placed on the taking of red fish in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and in view of the concern on the part of the fisheries
March 5, 1976

industry and the provincial governments of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland which have requested that the restriction be deferred until they can review its impact would the minister indicate whether he has agreed to that representation and what action he will take on it?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED
subsubtopic: FISH IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for having been absent when the hon. member first rose. This matter of the red fish had been made known in 1973 at a meeting in St. John's, Newfoundland and it produced then fairly dramatic headlines. At the time it was indicated that by 1975 the stocks would be depleted. Better management, with the help of the industry, allowed us to stretch the stock into 1976. However, we are now looking at the spawning stocks and no one in the industry wants us to destroy that part of the fishery. The quota limitations that were announced were hinted at very clearly in December of last year.
At the request of the industry, a scientific report was produced on February 11. When it was brought in, it was very pessimistic and therefore action had to be taken. The industry knew that there would be serious limitations in the quota this year. The large trawlers which were fishing in the gulf went to the level of their percentage of the quota in comparison with the previous years. Had we not intervened to close the red fish fishery now, there would have been nothing left for those vessels which are based in the gulf. They do not have the capacity to go outside the gulf and therefore would have had nothing left at all when their time came to fish in May.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED
subsubtopic: FISH IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: As the minister stated, the fact is that everybody knew that this fishery was being seriously depleted. As a matter of fact, in 1973 it amounted to 163,000 metric tons and in 1974 it went down to 63,000 metric tons. Would the minister explain why action was not taken at that time, action which would have been less severe, and would he also explain why Canada agreed at the ICNAF meetings to 90,000 metric tons quota, 60,000 metric tons of which went to the Russians? Is this reasonable with regard to Canadian fishermen and the future of our fishing industry?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED
subsubtopic: FISH IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope you will be patient with me because my explanation might take longer than I would like. The 1973 information was based on the class 1956-58 fish which were by then mature and which had to be caught, otherwise they would have died of old age.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED
subsubtopic: FISH IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED

speechtext: That is what the Liberal government is doing.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED

speechtext: Lest the explanation might die of old age as well-

subsubtopic: FISH IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION

-I wonder if we are not starting a series of questions that should properly be asked of the minister

when the estimates are before the standing committee. I think an expanded explanation is in order and I do not wish to interfere, but if we are to pursue the matter vigorously, it might be done there, unless there is a brief explanation.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED
subsubtopic: FISH IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: These fish were competing for food supplies with other fish and everybody accepted they had to be taken until we had reached the level of the spawning stock. This level has now been reached, and that is why we had to apply conservation measures. This is a gulf of St. Lawrence quota and is a strictly Canadian managed fishery. Foreign fleets are not fishing directly for red fish in the gulf, and it has no immediate relation with the IGNAF quota.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED
subsubtopic: FISH IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Regardless of what the minister says, the fishing industry in Newfoundland is almost obliterated and it will mean the loss of hundreds of jobs to fishermen. Is the minister taking into consideration the depressing effect on the economy of Newfoundland, and has he consulted with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion in order to provide some input or is he himself considering any compensation to the fishermen?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DEFERRAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON TAKING RED
subsubtopic: FISH IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: It must be pointed out that although the red fish fishery is closed, the fishermen can fish other species in the gulf, such as cod. The industry has known about the coming reduction and it certainly can adjust to it, as fishermen in Nova Scotia have adjusted to the three months closure of the haddock fishery at spawning time. We have an assistance program for the fisheries, including some assistance which will be announced in the next few days. The industry at this point has caught its share of red fish and it simply must adapt itself to others having their share, too.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: USE OF POLYURETHANE FOAM IN CANADIAN NUCLEAR INSTALLATIONS
speechtext: Atomic Energy of Canada Limited reports as follows: Polyurethane foam has limited use in all current CANDU designs. It is used in a limited number of applications where a high quality vapour barrier is required and in some cases this includes openings through which electrical cables pass. In no case is it used as a seal at the main containment boundary. It is not used as insulation for cables or equipment. The potential hazards of its use have always been recognized and precautions taken to minimize the risk of fire.

speechtext: Order, please. The House is resuming debate on motion No. 2 in the name of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), and motion No. 3 in the name of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro).

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we concluded last night I was trying in my own quiet way to give the government a bit of hell for ignoring the maritime code and the opportunity to strengthen that portion of the bill dealing with cabotage. In the event that I did not put it on the record last night, and in order to refresh the minds of hon. members, my amendment is as follows:
"Canada: and, for better ensuring the attainment of the said purposes, any port or place in the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon shall be deemed to be a port or place in Canada, and the governor in council may, by order, provide that any other port or place not in Canada shall be deemed to be in Canada,".
In committee, the departmental officials assured us there is protection with regard to foreign ships coming into Canada, picking up tourists, travelling to other ports, touching at a foreign port, in this case St. Pierre and Miquelon, and returning to Canada. In our opinion, that assurance is not clear in the act. The amendment is to clause 8. It would delete line 20 at page 12 of the bill. It is our submission that this particular clause could be construed or interpreted in more than one way. I quote from the clause:
For the purposes of this section and sections 9 to 14, the "coasting trade of Canada" includes
(a) the carriage of goods by water or by land and water, the carriage
of passengers by water, and towage,
(i)	from one port or place in Canada to the same or another port or place in Canada,
(ii)	between a port or place in Canada and any marine structure that is engaged in exploration for or exploitation of natural resources in accordance with a permit or licence issued pursuant to an act of parliament or of the legislature of a province .. .
whether directly or by way of a foreign port-
It is that which gives us cause for concern. There are ample precedents in other statutes of Canada: it is spelled out very, very clearly. This amendment and the parallel amendment of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) would state in no uncertain terms what we understand to be the intent of parliament, the drafter and the act. By using the gimmick of stopping at a foreign port en route, foreign cruise ships-Russian, in the case of the east coast-can get around that section of the marine code directed to the closing of the coasting trade of Canada for Canadian ships with Canadian crews.
The amendment, as I say, is in two parts. What we seek to do is simply to declare that for the purposes of the act, St. Pierre and Miquelon are parts of Canada. It has become obvious that the Canadian cruise industry has been destroyed by the operations of Soviet cruise ships carried on without regard for any normal commercial considerations. Cruises are carried on in the Gulf of the St. Lawrence, on the Saguenay River and out to the coastal waters of Newfoundland with stop-offs at St. Pierre and Miquelon. Soviet ships are permitted to do this by reason of the loophole in the existing law.
March 5, 1976

We submit that the code is vague to a degree unacceptable to us in this regard. What these vessels do is make a 10-hour or 12-hour stop-over at some foreign port. All they have to do is sail from a Canadian port to a foreign port; this enables them to satisfy the letter of the code and we regard it as a way of getting around the requirement of this particular section since, technically, the voyage has become an international voyage.
Comments were made by other speakers last night with respect to the carriage of goods from the east coast to the west coast of Canada. Certain problems were envisaged. Mr. Speaker, the amendment changes only slightly the definition found in the old Canada Shipping Act. We suggest that the present provisions are not adequate to provide the type of protection the code should contain. The amendment would simply eliminate any ground for dispute.
The second part of the amendment gives the governor in council authority to designate other foreign ports or places to be, for the purposes of the act, ports within Canada. This would enable the cabinet to intervene with respect to certain situations which arise on the Great Lakes when ships picking up Canadian tourists are able to take Canadian dollars from our own tourist industry. It would also enable the cabinet to intervene in the case of similar practices on the west coast.
To illustrate the seriousness of the situation, I would put on record the statements made by various witnesses who appeared before the committee. It is estimated that in the tourist industry alone, between 300 and 500 jobs are lost to Canadian sailors, suppliers, shipbrokers, and so on, because Canada cannot compete with offshore companies which operate in our waters without regard to the profit motive. The president of the Seafarers' International Union had this to say when he appeared before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, as reported in the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence for December 11, 1975:
Cruises in Canada, even if they include St. Pierre and Miquelon or U.S. ports, should be explicitly reserved for Canadian ships.
In recent years, foreign cruise ships have increasingly been operating in Canada. On the west coast, this has resulted in the replacement of vessels manned by Canadians. In the east, Danish and U.S.S.R. flag ships are operating St. Lawrence River cruises. They leave Montreal and sail to Quebec, Bagotville, Perce, with a perfunctory stop at St. Pierre and Miquelon. The passengers disembark to sightsee at the various ports. We have contended that there are violations in the present laws regarding the coasting trade ...
The emphasis he placed on the lack of Canadian jobs is significant in light of the amendment. As I say, several hundred jobs are affected directly and indirectly. I can see no reason why such a simple amendment should not be taken into serious consideration by the government. We are not attempting to impose upon that French colony or, indeed, on any other foreign port, the laws and regulations of Canada. We are simply saying, for the purposes of this act, that those ports should not be designated as foreign ports, thus getting around the loophole in the old Canada Shipping Act and in the new Maritime Code.
I maintain the amendment should enjoy the support of all hon. members and is a necessary one if we are to lend to the act the spirit which I am sure it is intended to reflect. This question has been before us for a long time. I might
Maritime Code
add that the amendment has been carefully drafted with regard to the uncertainties and fears felt by the council of maritime premiers and by representatives of British Columbia ports with respect to the impact it might have on freight costs.
We need further assurances which will satisfy the council of maritime premiers and the government of Newfoundland as well as British Columbia interests. We need a forthright statement from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to the effect that the assurances given by his predecessor to the council of maritime premiers in Charlottetown some 18 months ago are, in fact, being carried out.
We would much prefer the government to have imported something in written form into this particular clause so as to give statutory authority to the type of protection required. Failure to do so has caused us some difficulty with respect to legislation which otherwise we on this side generally support. We reserve our right to make a final decision with respect to the attitude we shall take toward third reading. I may say it will depend to a large degree upon the type of assurance the Minister of Transport is able to give us. The issue is an important one to the thousands of men and women whose lives are directly related to maritime activity, as well as to the country as a whole. The Maritime Code is too valuable a piece of legislation to allow to go by without our calling attention to the fact that it contains major loopholes through which Russian cruise ships can take away dollars and cents from Canadians.
What we will be attempting to do by this amendment is to strengthen and clarify the legislation and remove uncertainty respecting the intent of the act, which is to provide the framework for the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine, one that will be slowly developed and will pay regard to the requirements of the competitive transportation of goods in this country. We do not suggest exclusively closing our waters in any place. We have always recognized that there will be situations where Canadian vessels are not available or where for one reason or another a specialized type of ship is required. This might be a cruise ship, an ore carrier, an ice strengthened bulk carrier for operations north of 60, and so on.
Canadian businessmen and entrepreneurs require ships when they need them, not six months afterwards. When the need arises, they require access to adequate means of transportation. So we do not interfere with the rights or principles that protect users, the governor in council can always consider the granting of a special permit. Were that not in the legislation, we would insist upon it.
Canada should have its own merchant fleet and I suggest that starting with the coastal trade is the right route. We are not going to see the development of a Canadian merchant fleet next year or within five years, but if we do not start somewhere we will never achieve this goal. The thousands of potential jobs in our shipyards, on board ship and in related industries are too important for us to permit legislation of this significance to go through without the assurance that it is tight, that it is not full of loopholes but reflects our desire to provide the framework within which Canadians can redevelop their merchant fleet, and lending

March 5, 1976
Maritime Code
institutions engaging in maritime activity can approach without fear those entrepreneurs prepared to invest their talent and credit in achieving this end.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address myself to motion No. 2 standing in the name of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). In this particular part of the act we are dealing with what amounts to the core of this legislation, the definition of "cabotage". We must be sure we mean what we say and that Canadian shipping is assured the right to cabotage.
During my remarks on second reading of the bill I went into the use of that term to a considerable extent, and I suggest we briefly review its meaning here. It originated, as I mentioned at the time, from the business of going from cape to cape. "Cabo" is from the Portuguese or Spanish, but it has been translated in much more definitive terms in air law. In air law we never accept that a non-Canadian carrier can pick up passengers in Canada, call at a U.S. port, drop them off, pick up additional passengers bound for Canada and call this a domestic flight. These flights have to be worked out very carefully in agreements.
We insist that between Canadian ports we will not have foreign carriers picking up passengers in Montreal and dropping them off in Toronto. This is reserved to Canadian carriers. This is the basic principle we are seeking to define much more rigidly in cabotage or, if you like, in the coasting trade. We are transferring it from air law back into maritime law from whence it came. I insist, Mr. Speaker, that without a full definition of "cabotage" as defined so precisely in air law and translated into maritime law, there can be no encouragement given the Canadian maritime industries, Canadian mariners, shipbuilders, provisioners, victuallers, and our steelworks as well, to provide Canadian bottoms for the carriage of Canada's coastal trade.
In connection with motion No. 2, it is easy to make a pro forma call at St. Pierre and Miquelon, saying that your voyage plan requires a stop-over or route stop, to convert a voyage from, say, Montreal, up the Saugenay via St. Pierre and Miquelon, from a Canadian trip in which cabotage should be the rule into an international voyage and therefore open to any carrier.
I cannot help wishing there were greater awareness in this chamber of the significance of St. Pierre and Miquelon. I was greatly helped by reading a book by a very prominent Canadian historian who is now attached to the University of Carleton at the Institute of International Affairs, Professor Douglas Anglin, who wrote a book entitled "The St. Pierre and Miquelon Affair". I commend the book to all members of the House. It relates the manner in which the Free French occupied St. Pierre and Miquelon during the Second World War and the problems this created for the then prime minister, which he faced in one particular way. But it also drew attention at the time to the significance of St. Pierre and Miquelon to Canada's geography and sovereignty.
We are now seeing a further significance in dealing with the law of the sea and the extension of our territorial and fishing limits out from our coastline. The mathematical and cartographical problems of extending southward from

St. Pierre and Miquelon their claim to territorial jurisdiction, in which French law will predominate, is a most complex question for anyone who has thought about it for more than two or three minutes. Recognizing that St. Pierre and Miquelon is within what would ordinarily be Canadian waters, recognizing that it is a blob of foreign territory within what are otherwise our territorial waters, we must consider that a call there will not convert a voyage from Montreal or Quebec, up the Saugenay with just a formal call at St. Pierre and Miquelon, into an international voyage but will be for all purposes a voyage in Canadian waters.
This same sort of operation occurs in the Great Lakes. It permits non-Canadian carriers, foreign carriers, to exploit an industry which, with the encouragement of a very strict cabotage rule, permits some carriers to enter the luxury trade, if you like, the summer cruise trade, simply by enabling a ship to call alternatively on one side of the St. Lawrence River or the other and convert that particular trip into an international voyage rather than a voyage through strictly Canadian waters.
Even a trip, let us say, from Thunder Bay to Sault Ste. Marie could be converted by making an intermediate call at Duluth. This is the sort of thing we would like to see closed in order to encourage Canadian ship-owners, shipbuilders and the whole maritime industry to build Canadian ships and give a start again to a Canadian marine industry so that we again will be a maritime power which our position, our coastline and our whole tradition dictates for us. We must do this before it is too late.
We have heard that there are difficulties in obtaining crews for Canadian vessels because of the cost. I have thrown out a suggestion to some of our marine architects. I have suggested there is a way perhaps to deal with this admittedly difficult problem of having the breadwinner away from home at sea for many, many months. I think the matter has been greatly facilitated by the introduction of the container ship. I suggested to this particular marine architect that it should be a simple matter to have standing on most container ports trailers which could be hoisted aboard in the same way a container is hoisted aboard. These could be fully equipped trailer camp homes. The crew could live in them. They could even take their families with them. There would no longer be the need to separate the breadwinner from the other members of the family, because the other members of the family could go on the voyage. The families would have the advantage of the education overseas which travel conveys. If enough of them were on board, it is conceivable that there could even be correspondence classes carried on for any children who might be there.
It might be of interest to know that in addition to this particular suggestion I was told by the naval architect with whom I was speaking that there is a movement among those industries in Canada which are concerned about naval architecture to establish at the University of British Columbia a special course in naval architecture. Such an institute of naval architecture at my alma mater would be a further sign of the intent of this country to proceed with the purpose this bill attempts to display,

namely, the creation, as I understand it, of a Canadian merchant marine.
I commend this notion to the government and suggest that if some application for assistance along these lines is made, it be favourably received. We must tighten up clause 8 of Bill C-61. We must have a definition of "cabotage" which is meaningful even, if necessary, by borrowing those concepts from air law and translating them into maritime law. We recognize that at least as an interim measure there is under subclause (5) the authority vested in the governor in council to permit exception, to carriers for specified purposes and for a specified time by way of an interim measure. That particular clause need not be there for all time, but only until such time as Canada's merchant marine is capable of standing on its own feet and carrying out the trade which is so important to the Canadian economy and to Canada as a trading nation.
This particular amendment, motion No. 2 in the name of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, deals with the trade on the east coast particularly, the cruising trade if you like; but there is also the merchant trade, the carriage of goods on the east coast, which has caused considerable concern, I understand, to the first ministers of the maritime provinces. They want assurance that if we tighten up the cabotage provisions in this particular legislation, there will still be competitive bids on the carriage of goods between the provinces, between the mainland and Newfoundland if you like, and up into Labrador. This is most important. We have mentioned it in other contexts and we will mention it again on many occasions.
We want assurance from the minister that the first ministers of the maritime provinces are in agreement with the regulations which are to be drawn up, I believe, under clause 12 of this bill. We mentioned in committee, as well, that members of parliament would like to see the regulations before this bill becomes law. I found it altogether surprising that so much of the legislation that is brought before us, legislation of a fundamental and basic kind such as this, contains provisions for the eventual appearance of regulations. I would like to think that we would get away from this practice. We have schedules I and II, and I believe there is also a schedule III here. Schedule III provides for Book I of the Maritime Code, and I suppose schedule IV provides for Book II. Why could there not be a schedule which contains the regulations?
The provisions of the code are fundamental. They are the ground rules under which Canadian ships and foreign ships will operate in Canadian waters. I think it is important that the regulations be published before this bill becomes law. For the time being I will reserve my comments on the amendment which stands in my name. There may be others who wish to comment further on this motion which has a bearing on the waters in the mouth of the St. Lawrence and on the east coast trade.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will continue my remarks now, but will direct them to the motion which stands in my name and which is of a more general nature but still deals with the cruising industry. It could also deal with the merchant industry on the west coast. I do not know how many members in the House have done the trip from the top of the island, from Kelsey Bay, up to Prince Rupert through the inland passage. It is a trip which is reminiscent of the Norwegian fiords for those who have travelled through the narrow waters with mountains coming right down on both sides. You feel, as you go through some of the passages, that if you stretched out far enough you could touch the shores on either side. The same applies up the coast beyond Prince Rupert. I am sorry that the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) is not here because I am sure that she would like to describe some of the beauties of this area.
Because these areas are so attractive they are great summer cruising areas which are being invaded by ships conducting international cruises. Therefore, we must have some provision within our definition of "cabotage" in this act to enable Canadian ships to get into the trade in this area as we were describing it on the east coast. It is a very simple matter which can be done in a variety of ways. A ship can load its passengers in Vancouver, let us say, go down Pugit Sound to Seattle to pick up some more passengers, then come up to Victoria. It is then involved in an international cruise, whether passengers have gone down and got off in Seattle or gone for a day's shopping and come up to Vancouver. Then the ship might go on through the inland passage, up through Johnson strait. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) is not here either, but he also knows this area. Instead of going from Vancouver directly to Prince Rupert, they could go on to Ketchikan and convert this interCanadian port cruise into an international cruise. This is exactly what has been happening and the trade on the west coast has been taken over.
My first sight of the Pacific was from a ship travelling from Vancouver up the west coast to Vancouver Island and to Zeballos for a summer job. This is one of the delights of the summer in that particular area. You can run into some rough weather, but in good weather it is a splendid trip and I commend it to anyone who can afford the time. But those trips are no longer possible. The Canadian ships have been taken off those particular journeys, unfortunately, because of the simplicity with which it is possible to convert a trip into an international voyage and therefore bring in a non-Canadian or non-American carrier to do the

March 5, 1976
Maritime Code
trip. At present it is the Norwegians and the Dutch who do this, if I remember correctly. There are a few others.
Sometimes some of the world cruise trips do part of the journey, but basically, on a back and forth deal between the extremities, it might be San Diego, San Fransisco, Vancouver, Ketchikan, Prince Rupert, and out farther into Alaska and then back down. This has been turned over because of the absence of a firm, solid definition of what cabotage is to foreign vesels. We see vessels coming in, as was mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for Dar-mouth-Halifax East, which are not even required to fulfil the standards of work within Canada. The workmen are not subject to our Workmen's Compensation Act and they are not paid the wages that Canadian workmen demand.
We should close the loopholes in this definition of "cabotage" so as to encourage Canadian shipping to resume those trips up the west coast, whether it be up the Pacific or up the inland passage. I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) had.done some of these trips from Vancouver, and he can testify to the great beauty of the trip and to the relaxation which a trip of that sort on a good ship can provide to anyone who is a little weary of life in the city and who seeks some way of being carried back to nature. But we will not do this on Canadian ships unless we close those loopholes in the law. That is the whole meaning of the amendment which I am putting forward.
I have used the word "cabotage" too much, but I think it has a meaning in English to which we should get back. The coasting trade is one thing, but it does not carry that connotation of "cabotage" which it does in air law. I think we must get it back into the maritime law where it came from and where it belongs. It is with that view in mind that these two amendments have been drafted.
There is one caveat here, Mr. Speaker, which was mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). There is a problem in intercoastal trade in Canadian bottoms. Let us say there could be a problem unless we have provision for competitive bidding, because when you load at Nanaimo, say, and offload at Dartmouth or St. John's, the quickest way of making the journey is, through the Panama Canal, winter or summer. I do not think you can do it the other way with a load of lumber. The Panama Canal, of course, means a call at a foreign port, which turns it into an international trip and therefore it is open to non-Canadian carriers.
We have to find some means-and we have not found it yet-of encouraging Canadian bottoms to get into that lucrative trade. It is a part of the Canadian business. I am sure it is still true that it is cheaper to carry goods by water than any other means, over long distances. Wheat, of course, cannot be carried any other way than by ships, but the carriage of goods by sea has historically been cheaper than carriage by any other means. Time is involved in going from the west coast to the east coast though the Panama Canal, but it should be cheaper to carry lumber, minerals or whatever commodity from the west coast across the continent by water than by rail.
There was some mention in the debate yesterday that if ships were in the hands of one of the railways, the water

rates would be increased to match the rail rates. Perhaps we should ensure there is encouragement to shippers, independent of the rails, to build Canadian ships and enter Canadian coastal trade from the west coast to the east coast.
Perhaps it is looking a long way ahead, but there has been mention of the trade that could develop in the Arctic. I was shocked to hear that consideration was being given to having ships built in German shipyards to take ore from the Canadian Arctic to Canadian refineries in the St. Lawrence. This is cabotage in its pureset form from the Canadian Arctic to Canadian mills and foundries whether they be in the St. Lawrence or up the Great Lakes. This trade should be carried by Canadian ships, manned by Canadian crews. We are not going to have that opportunity until we give encouragement with law and with subsidies. I think we must face the fact that subsidies will be required to encourage a Canadian maritime service to get Canadian vessels back into the trade, particularly in Canada. From there we can expand to the wider, lucrative trade of carrying Canadian goods to international ports.
The Norwegians do not lose money in this type of trade. They have very high standards of seamanship and shipbuilding, and are making money. Why should the Canadian industry not be doing the same? This is the reason we have been seeking to tighten the meaning of clause 8 so that the need to invoke section 5 will become less and less frequent as the years go by. In the course of time we would like section 5 to be no longer necessary because cabotage would mean exactly what it ought to mean, namely, reserving to Canadians the right to carry goods from one Canadian port to another. There are strange anomalies in our geography, in the history of the development of our continent such as we see in St. Pierre and Miquelon, and in the geographic and diplomatic anomaly of the appearance of the Alaska Panhandle, which cut off a great part of the north of our provinces from the sea by an award in the nineteenth century. Those anomalies exist and we have to accept them. Since they exist, we should be able to provide the appropriate wording in the law to overcome them.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will call it one o'clock.

speechtext:
Motion No. 4.
That Bill C-61, an act to provide a maritime code for Canada, to amend the Canada Shipping Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential or related provisions, be amended in clause 10 by deleting lines 31 and 32 at page 14 and substituting the following therefor:
"renewal or terminating later than September 24, 1978".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will see if it is possible to get another 35 or 40 minutes out of a one-liner. Years ago when I was working for the Halifax Herald, being taught by a now distinguished deputy minister of the government of Nova Scotia, I would be called into the newsroom because it was my job for a long time to make an eight or ten paragraph story out of some little news release. I do not know whether I learned my lesson well.
The purpose of this motion is to attempt to give some recognition to the notice given by the government under the former minister of transport to our member Commonwealth countries of our intention to withdraw from the Commonwealth shipping arrangement. The act calls for a termination date in April of 1980, and I am suggesting that it be on September 24, 1978. Notice of this intention was formally served on the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth nations which participate in the Commonwealth shipping arrangements in 1973.
We suggest that we withdraw from these arrangements on September 24, 1978, for a variety of reasons. It is many years since those interested in the redevelopment of a Canadian merchant marine initiated the action that we are discussing in parliament today. There can be no occasion for any shipping company operating under a Commonwealth flag to complain that they were not adequately forewarned of our intention, of which notice was served in 1973. We are fully in accordance with the five-year notice and we went through the one-year period before formal notice could be given. Formal notice was then given that we would subsequently withdraw from the Commonwealth shipping arrangement.
In support of my argument I should like to quote briefly from the evidence given to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications on December 11, 1975, at

March 5, 1976
Maritime Code
page 30:7. These words were introduced into the record by the president of the Seafarer's International Union and were also endorsed by the CBRT:
Third, grandfather rights set out in clause 10 should expire on September 23, 1978.
In 1973, the then minister of transport announced a policy restricting the coasting trade of Canada to Canadian ships and indicated that there would be a five-year period of grandfather rights in favour of the British ships then engaged in the coasting trade. We think the five-year period should commence from September 24, 1973, which was the date of his announcement, or at the very latest, from the date on which notice was given to the Commonwealth countries that Canada was withdrawing from the Commonwealth Shipping Agreement, which was on April 26, 1974.
He then went on to urge the committee to give consideration to this matter, and I think the committee did give it consideration. I appreciate the arguments that have been put forward on the matter by the parliamentary secretary, bolstered by their expert witness, Mr. Maloney, that from the point of view of formality the later date was the best date to follow. However, our reaction is somewhat different. We have been trying for 15 to 20 years to re-establish the framework within which we can redevelop not only a foreign deep sea fleet but strengthen and bolster the existing coastal shipping capacity and capability which Canada has.
Most of Canada's trade is now carried in Canadian ships, so there is not going to be any great problem here. I think 75 to 80 per cent of our export trade, not only today but traditionally, has always been carried in Canadian ships, so not too many ships are going to be affected. The hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) yesterday expressed to the House fears he had about interference or intervention with competitive rates for the movement of goods. That aspect is present and we do not treat it lightly, but what I am saying is that so far as our coastal trade is concerned the matter is not significantly important. A relatively small percentage of our coastal trade is carried in other than Canadian registered and crewed ships.
Where this does have an impact is that it affects, morally-and, I suppose, philosophically-our approach to the development of a Canadian merchant marine. Canada had some 452 registered ships serving in liner conferences alone in and out of our country last year. If we went to the UNCTAD arrangement and the new code of ethics for liner conferences, in terms of securing forever 40 per cent of our incoming and outgoing export traffic it would mean 175 Canadian ships. Under the UNCTAD arrangement, 55 per cent of the major carriers of the world have already endorsed this particular proposal, but this is getting a little far afield from the date of withdrawal from the Commonwealth shipping arrangement.
I am attempting to draw to the attention of the House that we are talking here about at least 7,000 new jobs for Canadians. For example, the Halifax shipyard in my own constituency will come to the end of the offshore oil drilling rig construction and development program some time within a year. What is going to happen to the 600 or 800 men who are going to be laid off? We are trying to create work for our shipyards. We are trying to create jobs for our seamen, merchant service officers and Canadian suppliers. We are talking about hard-earned money. A total of $2.7 billion is being given away to the cartels in Toyko, New York, London and Athens. I want this to come home to

Canada, not in 15 years or in 10 years but as soon as it can be done in an orderly fashion. I want us to hold strong to this point.
Someone might ask what difference it makes whether the anniversary date is 1978 or 1980. Probably the only difference it makes is that it points out to the people of the world that we are serious in our intention to keep some of this amount of $2.7 billion for our own use rather than give it away. A number of recommendations were made by the somewhat scholarly report of the Darling commission in respect of an international shipping structure for Canada. I am sure members of the House have read this report. Some interesting comments were made in respect of Canada's position if we continue to rely on foreign shipping.
There are some interesting comments and observations about our procrastination in this regard. It is pointed out that we must not only be doing these things, but we must be seen to be doing them. We have the situation of our wood being shipped from British Columbia to Japan in Japanese ships. Our lumber from the west coast is being shipped on vessels of foreign registration. Our potatoes are being shipped from New Brunswick to the United States, to the Caribbean and to Europe in foreign registered ships. Why? By taking the extreme end in establishing the anniversary date beyond which the grandfather rights will not apply, except in the absence of a suitable Canadian ship, we are seeming to say to these countries that they can carry on and use our dollars because we need their vessels. We have heard the argument that we really cannot compete offshore in respect of exports because of the cost of a crew. That was true 40 years ago, but it is an insignificant factor now in respect of today's highly automated vessels and ships. It really is not an argument.
I come back again to the position in which we find ourselves. We are saying, in effect, to the countries of the world that we will do this even if it takes 100 years. We should tell the world we intend to do it as quickly and efficiently as we can, and that the delay will only be for two or three years. This probably is a relatively minor point I am making. However, what is at stake is a substantial Canadian industry. Every other significant transport industry in Canada today is protected and subsidized. But this industry for a long time has been treated as an accident of circumstance, while in fact it is an integral industry; it is a major industry in Canada. We are talking about
14,000	seamen and another 3,000 to 5,000 officers and engineers. Any industry which employs 14,000 people is a substantial contributor to the Canadian economy. Let us tell the people around the world who are hauling our exports because it costs them a few dollars less for a crew, with the exception of the Russians and one or two other countries, that we intend to do it ourselves, not at some point in the future but at the first possible opportunity.
I suggest that notice was clearly given to the countries of the world, particularly the Commonwealth countries which are members of and were participants in the Commonwealth agreement, that we want to see that amount of $2.7 billion which we lose in the form of transportation costs revert to the Canadian consumer and come back to the government which can squander it, if you like. We want it to come back to Canada so that it might be the
March 5, 1976

basis upon which we can build our own Canadian merchant fleet and develop it in an orderly fashion so that it will not disrupt or disorient the competitive movement of our goods.
I commend these points to the chamber because they are important. I suggest this amendment is a simple attempt to make known to the foreign cartels which operate at our expense, and who make it difficult for us to get on with what we intend to do, that we are serious and intend to move in as quick and orderly a fashion as we can. I hope other members will have observations to make in this regard because it is important that people understand we are serious and intend to move.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). Again I would say to the House that we had the benefit of very substantial argument on his particular points during our committee hearings. He has read into the record some of the proceedings in respect of this matter. Clause 10 of the bill refers to what we call in shorthand the "grandfather rights," the rights which exist in respect of certain vessels which have been in the coasting trade of Canada to continue in that trade.
I was happy to hear my friend across the way agree with the basic concept of those rights continuing for a five-year period. There does not seem to be any dispute about that. I gather his argument is for a stronger appearance or a stronger impression. His only argument seems to be that somehow we should go back to an earlier base date in calculating those five years than the one which may be the more proper formal date. Perhaps, for the information of members, it would be useful to explain the difference between the two dates. I think the date to which my hon. friend refers is September 24, 1973. This is the date upon which the former minister of transport issued a statement in conjunction with his colleagues from the Atlantic provinces following a meeting at Summerside, Prince Edward Island.
On that occasion the minister indicated that the government of Canada would be withdrawing from the British Commonwealth merchant shipping agreement. That was a general indication of intention at that particular moment of time in 1973. I would say to the members of the House that in my view that falls substantially short of what in law and justice would amount to formal notice.
At some time later, on April 26, 1975, the formal notice was served by Canada, as is required under the agreement which I have just mentioned, the British Commonwealth merchant shipping agreement, of our intention to withdraw from the terms of that agreement. So in the first instance we have a general statement of principle or of intention issued in the form of a press statement or a communique in September of 1973, followed by the required legal or international action which was necessary on our part in 1975 to accomplish in law what we indicated we would eventually be doing after September of 1973.
Maritime Code
The fact remains that the necessary legal steps could not be accomplished until a later date, that is until 1975, and it seems to me that it is far more than just a formality or perhaps the more polite way to proceed; it is, indeed, the legal and proper way for us to proceed to look at the later date, that is, the date in 1975, as the basic date for the calculation of those five years for the purposes of the so-called grandfather rights preserved in clause 10. We should not, and indeed cannot, go back to the earlier date in 1973 for the basis of that calculation. For these reasons, I think it is necessary and important that the House not accept this particular amendment which would terminate those rights in 1978, but in fact leave the statute in the words in which it is now phrased where those rights would expire in 1980.
